subject: physics
title: Energy Levels and Line Spectra
welcome_lead: Climb the hydrogen ladder and emit a photon at every step down.
meta_desc: A-Level Quantum adventure on atomic energy levels and emission/absorption spectra.
final_note: Discrete levels mean discrete photons — every element's barcode.

concepts.def: Discrete allowed energy of an electron.
Photon released when electron drops level.

walkthroughs.body_html: Electron energies are quantised: E_n = -13.6 eV / n². Negative because bound. n = 1 is ground state, n = ∞ is ionisation.
Drop from E₂ to E₁ releases a photon of energy hf = E₂ - E₁. Different transitions give different colours: Balmer series is visible, Lyman is UV.
Hot, low-density gas emits at specific wavelengths (bright lines). Cool gas in front of a continuous source absorbs at the same wavelengths (dark Fraunhofer lines).

Why do atoms emit light only at specific wavelengths rather than a continuous spectrum?
options: Intensity has no effect on anything in the photoelectric effect.
Atoms emit only one colour each, determined by their temperature.
Atoms can emit any wavelength, but only certain ones are visible.
Electrons occupy discrete energy levels; transitions between levels emit photons of specific frequencies (E = hf).

mcqs.q: What determines the energy of a single photon?
options: Photon energy depends on how fast the photon is moving relative to the source.
A brighter light has higher-energy photons because intensity makes each photon more energetic.
Its frequency (E = hf) — only frequency, not intensity.
Atoms emit only one colour each, determined by their temperature.

mcqs.q: How does the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons depend on light intensity?
options: Higher intensity gives photoelectrons more kinetic energy.
Atoms emit only one colour each, determined by their temperature.
It does not — max KE depends only on the frequency of the light; intensity affects the rate (number) of electrons emitted.
Intensity has no effect on anything in the photoelectric effect.
